title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Quality control for and normalizing of high dimension single nuclear transcriptomic data
text:
Explore the SingleCellExperiment Object

Dimensions: Rows and columns
Rows correspond to features – another term for genes. At this point though, they may represent exons or introns since we’re working with single nuclear data.
Columns correspond to droplets – right now they’re termed “droplets” because we may have empty droplets or doublets. After filtering, these droplets can also be termed nuclei for snRNA-seq data because we assume we’ve removed the droplets without single nuclei.

What are the dimensions of the object?


dim(snrna_data)

[1] 87308 65989
So that’s 87,308 features and 65,989 droplets.
By the time that we’re done with filtering, we expect to have a lot more nuclei than we do genes. This is because single cell data is very sparse typically. More on this later (even within this exploration section), but briefly:

Genes currently in the SingleCellExperiment object could represent mitochondrial genes – we don’t want those because we’re working with single nuclear data
(Add a dropdown section on why single cell data may be interested in mitochondrial reads)
Genes also may be listed more than once right now – exon and intron versions
There could be non-informative genes (low or no counts across droplets)

We will be filtering out some droplets (empty from ambient RNA detection and doublets from doublet detection), but filtering resources advise liberally keeping droplets when possible.


Metadata and Data

Show how to look at the column metadata


colData(snrna_data)

DataFrame with 65989 rows and 2 columns
                 whitelist   sample_id
                 <logical> <character>
TTCGCTGCAAGTCGTT      TRUE          1C
TATGTTCCACTATGTG      TRUE          1C
AGGGTCCTCCAGCCTT      TRUE          1C
CACATGACATCGGTTA      TRUE          1C
GCAGTGGTATCAACGC      TRUE          1C
...                    ...         ...
CCTCACAGTCTGTAGT     FALSE          8E
GAGAAATCAAGTGACG     FALSE          8E
GCAGCTGAGGCACTAG     FALSE          8E
GGGCTCATCGAAGTGG     FALSE          8E
CCGGTGACACTTGAAC     FALSE          8E
What metadata is currently there?

whitelist is a salmon alevin output from alignment and quantification of the reads, suggesting if that program thinks that the droplet should be kept (TRUE) or not (FALSE). We’ll compare our final filtering to this later in the Data Wrangling section (or as a basic suggested exercise?).
sample_id provides the ID for the samples, relating to which droplets were part of sequencing which samples. (In the narrative, especially make note that the Sample ID information is column metadata meaning that it connects to the droplets rather than the features (rows))

Note that the row names for the metadata above are the droplet IDs or “cell barcodes”. They look like a DNA sequence and that’s because they represent the specific nucleotide sequences attached to beads in each droplet that allow for molecules to be tagged or identified as originating from the same cell: https://www.10xgenomics.com/blog/how-does-single-cell-rna-seq-work
Any additional metadata that we want to add for this dataset will be added to the colData. We can access colData metadata one of two ways:

colData(snrna_data)$sample_id
snrna_data$sample_id


Show what samples there are


unique(snrna_data$sample_id)

[1] "1C" "2E" "3C" "4E" "5C" "8E"
Note that every Sample ID either has a C or an E in the ID

ncol(snrna_data) == sum(str_detect(snrna_data$sample_id, "C|E"))

[1] TRUE

Focus on droplets

Confirm how many droplets there are

Looking at the number of rows from the colData above and our dimensions earlier, we confirm that there are currently 65,989 droplets represented in this dataset.

Show how many droplets there are per sample


table(snrna_data$sample_id)

1C    2E    3C    4E    5C    8E
11000 10997 10999 10994 11000 10999
(if we add the numbers together from the table, we’ll also get the same number of droplets we saw earlier, so every droplet is assigned to a sample).

ncol(snrna_data) == sum(table(snrna_data$sample_id))

[1] TRUE


Focus on features

What are stored in the rows?


rowData(snrna_data)

We see that this is information about the features or the genes.
How do these columns get added to the SummarizedExperimentObject? … need to add

Where are the gene names?

The gene names are both the rownames and stored in the gene_id column of the rowData() output.
Notice that the gene IDs begin with “ENSMUSG” which tells us that they are Ensembl (ENS) Mus musculus (MUS) stable gene (trailing G) IDs.
Source: https://useast.ensembl.org/Help/Faq?id=488
Every row has that part of the ID at the beginning:

sum(str_detect(rownames(snrna_data), "^ENSMUSG")) == nrow(snrna_data)

[1] TRUE

Show how many genes there are

From the number of rows in the output from rowData() as well as the dimension beforehand, there are 87,308 features represented in this data.
However, of these features, some of the “genes” are listed more than once because both its exons and introns are represented. Notice the “-I” above at the end of the gene_id column. That signifies an intron.

sum(str_detect(rownames(snrna_data), "ENSMUSG00000095366"))

[1] 2
If we look specifically at the genes IDs for those 2 using which …

rownames(snrna_data)[which(str_detect(rownames(snrna_data), "ENSMUSG00000095366"))]

[1] "ENSMUSG00000095366.2"   "ENSMUSG00000095366.2-I"

We can look at how many features are representing an intron


sum(str_detect(rownames(snrna_data), "-I$"))

[1] 32961
If we were to just focus on the base ID (everything before the .## representing the version information for that feature), we can see how many unique genes are represented in this data
To do this, let’s remove everything period and after (that includes the numbers and the -I when present). This is the same as replacing all of that with an empty string ""

pattern_to_remove <- "\\..*"
replace_string <- ""

length(unique(sub(pattern_to_remove, replace_string, rownames(snrna_data))))

That leaves us with 54,464 unique genes represented in this data prior to filtering.
[1] 54464
(add a dropdown section about why we might filter genes specifically and not just droplets and point to section in data wrangling that does that)

Grab a random mitochondrial gene to show that there are some in the data

Random Mitochondrial gene ENSMUSG00000064351: https://useast.ensembl.org/Mus_musculus/Gene/Strain_Compara_Ortholog?g=ENSMUSG00000064351;r=MT:5328-6872;t=ENSMUST00000082402
“Mitochondrially encoded cytochrome c oxidase I”
Can confirm this ID is in this dataset

[1] 1
But unlike the introns, there’s nothing special about the gene ID for us to connect this gene to the Mitochondria.

rownames(snrna_data)[which(str_detect(rownames(snrna_data), "ENSMUSG00000064336"))]

[1] "ENSMUSG00000064336.1"

rowData(snrna_data)[which(str_detect(rownames(snrna_data), "ENSMUSG00000064336")), "SYMBOL"]

Focus on counts data

Show how to look at the counts data

There are three ways to access the counts data for a SingleCellExperiment object.

assays(snrna_data)$counts
assay(snrna_data, "counts")
counts(snrna_data)
Note that snrna_data$counts won’t work and returns NULL

ENSMUSG00000099619.6-I                .                .                .                .    ...
ENSMUSG00000099399.6-I                .                .                .                .    ...

Zeros or sparse representation?

The preview tells you that this is a “sparse” matrix meaning that it doesn’t store zeros, instead storing only non-zero values as well as locations where those non-zero values belong in the matrix. Instead of displaying a zero, it will display a . when you view the object/matrix.
Point to and explain this documentation: https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/Matrix/versions/1.7-4/topics/sparseMatrix
There are a lot of zero values in this data!! Very sparse!

non_zero_vals <- counts(snrna_data)@x #grabs just the non-zero data
prod(dim(snrna_data)) - length(non_zero_vals)

5579821106

Whole numbers or decimals?

Surprisingly, the counts matrix does not store whole numbers / integers only, but rather it can contain decimal values (also known as “doubles” in R). That’s because salmon is finding gene level estimates
Resources:

https://www.seqanswers.com/forum/bioinformatics/bioinformatics-aa/326416-nf-core-rnaseq-produces-non-integer-counts-in-salmon-merged-gene_counts-tsv
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6437997/

That’s not to say there aren’t whole numbers …. it’s just that there are decimals too

length(non_zero_vals) #this is the number of value that aren't zero

[1] 181546506

sum(non_zero_vals %% 1 == 0) #these are the number of estimates that are whole numbers

[1] 142611235

181546506 - 142611235 # these are the number of estimates that are decimals

[1] 38935271



Visualizing these “counts” …













rowSums … what does it represent? quantiles?

rowSums() is representing the sum of counts for a feature across droplets.

quantile(rowSums(assays(snrna_data)$counts))

0%          25%          50%          75%         100%
0.0000       0.0000      20.0000     883.4077 4036226.0377
We see that some features have 0 counts across droplets. These are non-informative features where we won’t be able to distinguish expression levels or patterns and how they might change according to condition, diagnosis, or treatment. Genes with consistently low counts (greater than 0) can still be non-informative, so often researchers will use a threshold approach to make sure that a sufficient number of droplets have at least a certain number of a counts (or greater) for features and filter out ones that don’t. A rowSums approach is necessary for this, and while it is still summing counts, those counts are compared to a threshold such that the following example will return a sum of TRUEs (1’s) and FALSEs (0’s) which are reporting if the observed number of counts is greater than the observed for each droplet for each feature. Specifically, for that feature, how many droplets have observed counts greater than the threshold.

title: Biomedical Open Case Studies: Quality control for and normalizing of high dimension single nuclear transcriptomic data
text:
Part 1: Data Preparation

Handling Introns and Exons

# Extract Exon Ensembl IDs and associated count data
exon_ids <- rowData(snrna_data) %>%
     as.data.frame() %>%
     dplyr::filter(!grepl("-I", gene_id)) %>%
     pull(gene_id)

exon_data <- snrna_data[exon_ids]

# Extract Intron Ensembl IDs and associated count data
intron_ids <- rowData(snrna_data) %>%
     as.data.frame() %>%
     dplyr::filter(grepl("-I", gene_id)) %>%
     pull(gene_id)

intron_data <- snrna_data[intron_ids]

# Simplify Ensembl IDs and find matching IDs between introns and exons

pattern_to_remove <- "\\..*"
replace_string <- ""

## the IDs
exon_ids <- sub(pattern_to_remove, replace_string, exon_ids)
intron_ids <- sub(pattern_to_remove, replace_string, intron_ids)

## the data sources
rownames(exon_data) <- exon_ids
rownames(intron_data) <- intron_ids
rownames(snrna_data) <- sub(pattern_to_remove, replace_string, rownames(snrna_data))

# Subset to only exons and introns with the same Ensembl ID
same_ensembl <- intersect(exon_ids, intron_ids)

# Remove introns and exons with shared IDs from the overall snRNA data
snrna_data_ids_subset <- rownames(snrna_data) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::filter(!. %in% same_ensembl) %>%
  pull(.)

# A new SingleCellExperiment object was created, where the sum
# of the UMI counts of spliced mRNA and introns sharing the same
# Ensembl ID was added.
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = rbind(counts(snrna_data[snrna_data_ids_subset]),
    counts(exon_data[same_ensembl]) + counts(intron_data[same_ensembl]))))

# Add back column and row data
colData(sce) <- colData(snrna_data)
rowData(sce) <- rbind(rowData(snrna_data) %>%
                        as.data.frame() %>%
                        dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% snrna_data_ids_subset),
                      rowData(snrna_data) %>%
                        as.data.frame() %>%
                        dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% same_ensembl)
                      )



# Add some more colData columns like condition and replicate number
sce <- sce %>%
  mutate(condition = case_when(str_detect(sample_id, "C") ~ "Control",
                               str_detect(sample_id, "E") ~ "SleepDeprived"
                               )
        ) %>%
  mutate(replicate = factor(str_remove(sample_id, "C|E")))



Annotate the chromosome including mitochondrial genes within rowData

map <- AnnotationDbi::mapIds(EnsDb.Mmusculus.v79, keys = rownames(sce), column = "SEQNAME",
               keytype = "GENEID")
rowData(sce)$CHR <- map
rowData(sce)$is_mito <- case_when(
  rowData(sce)$CHR == "MT"  ~ TRUE,
  .default = FALSE
)


Warning message: Unable to map 13156 of 54464 requested IDs.

Note that the number of rows matched the length of map though.
Let’s reclaim some environment space since we won’t need snrna_data again … removing the large data sets.

rm(snrna_data)
rm(exon_data)
rm(intron_data)

We can also remove some of the less large, but still sizable objects which are unnecessary moving forward

rm(exon_ids)
rm(intron_ids)
rm(map)
rm(same_ensembl)
rm(snrna_data_ids_subset)



Create SingleCellExperiment objects for each mouse
Ambient RNA detection is run on each sample separately, so we want to separate out the samples

sce_list <- split(sce, sce$sample_id)
names(sce_list) <- make.names(names(sce_list)) #if we don't do this, the names begin with a number and we won't be able to as easily access the different samples
names(sce_list)

[1] "X1C" "X2E" "X3C" "X4E" "X5C" "X8E"

Part 2: Quality Control
Add instructions on importing data in case people took a break and pick back up here.

Ambient RNA detection
Note that Ambient RNA detection should occur before any other filtering (I think even before filtering of non-informative (count 0) genes) because the algorithms rely on being able to model the background distribution of reads.
The classical plot to evaluate whether there may be Ambient RNA in your sample is the Barcode Rank plot that visualizes the total UMI or read counts for each barcode against the barcode’s rank (highest to lowest).
Note that though I’m using all of the samples together to make the plot, according to the OSCA book, we want to run ambient RNA detection tools on each sample separately because each sample will have a unique ambient RNA landscape and the tools (at least many of them) are comparing the total counts for each barcode against the total counts for the suspected ambient RNA population to decide what is an “empty” droplet vs a droplet with the data you want.
This approach utilizes base R to find the total counts and ranks (because DropletUtils wasn’t installing properly for me at first).

# 1. Calculate total counts (UMIs) per barcode (column)
total_counts <- Matrix::colSums(assays(sce)$counts)
# 2. Filter out barcodes with 0 counts (for speed)
total_counts <- total_counts[total_counts > 0]
# 3. Create a sorted data frame of unique counts and their ranks
bcranks <- data.frame(
Total = sort(total_counts, decreasing = TRUE),
Rank = seq_along(total_counts)
)
# 4. Remove duplicates
bcrank_unique <- bcranks[!duplicated(bcranks$Total), ]
# 5.
bcrank_unique %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=Rank, y = Total)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("Barcode Rank") +
  ylab("Total UMI Count") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_bw()










This approach utilizes DropletUtils to compute the sums and barcode ranks

ranks <- DropletUtils::barcodeRanks(sce)
uniq <- !duplicated(ranks$rank)
ranks_uniq <- ranks[uniq,]
ranks_uniq %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = total)) +
  geom_point() +
  xlab("Barcode Rank") +
  ylab("Total UMI Count") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  scale_y_log10() +
  theme_bw()










Both plots look the same and the tools that I’ve used either suggest keeping every droplet, or won’t run because it estimates that too much of the sample is contamination. This is the case for SoupX which suggested that the estimated contamination level was high (which is to be expected from snRNA-seq data): https://github.com/constantAmateur/SoupX/issues/76.
Therefore, I’m turning to a tool that was designed specifically for this task in snRNA-seq data. DIEM or “Debris Identification using Expectation Maximization”.
Working on running this within a script for each sample instead of an interactive session since the EM step takes quite a bit of time.

test_sce <- create_SCE(assays(sce_list[["1C"]])$counts)

# Plot total counts ranked
barcode_rank_plot(test_sce)

# DIEM steps
diem_sce_1c <- set_debris_test_set(test_sce)
diem_sce_1c <- filter_genes(diem_sce_1c)
diem_sce_1c <- get_pcs(diem_sce_1c)
diem_sce_1c <- init(diem_sce_1c)
diem_sce_1c <- run_em(diem_sce_1c)
diem_sce_1c <- assign_clusters(diem_sce_1c)
diem_sce_1c <- estimate_dbr_score(diem_sce_1c)

# Evaluate debris scores
sm <- summarize_clusters(diem_sce_1c)
plot_clust(diem_sce_1c, feat_x = "n_genes", feat_y = "score.debris",
           log_x = TRUE, log_y = FALSE)
plot_clust(diem_sce_1c, feat_x = "pct.mt", feat_y = "score.debris",
           log_x = TRUE, log_y = FALSE)

# Call targets using debris score for single-nucleus data
diem_sce_1c <- call_targets(diem_sce_1c, thresh_score = 0.5)

# Call targets by removing droplets in debris cluster(s) for single-cell data
diem_sce_1c <- call_targets(diem_sce_1c, clusters = "debris", thresh = NULL)

Likely will provide filtering output suggestions from DIEM (if there are any) to learners using a cooking show approach rather than having them run it themselves.


Filter for non-informative genes

rowData(sce)$keep_informative <- rowSums(assays(sce)$counts > 0) > 10
table(rowData(sce)$keep_informative)

FALSE  TRUE
23521 30943
What thresholds is appropriate here? This code is currently finding genes that have a non-zero count in at least 11 droplets. As described in this resource, we want to make sure we’re not potentially removing the ability to detect rare cell types and we might be able to use clustering to help tune this number


And when is the right time to do this step filtering out non-informative genes? I’m fairly certain after ambient RNA detection and before normalization I would expect, but I’m not sure if it needs to be before other QC steps as well.
Note that my computational environment struggles unless I constantly overwrite sce. To increase feasibility, I think

we need to show learners how to remove large things we won’t need again from the environment
avoid writing intermediates (like sce_filter)



Use perCellQCMetrics to identify low quality or damaged droplets
(rename this heading because of need for different function)

… Adding a summary of the data wrangling steps directly related to data handling in this section that I propose we use (since above this section I showed methods that either didn’t take batch into account or used deprecated functions)

# Data Prep

exon_ids <- rowData(snrna_data) %>%
     as.data.frame() %>%
     dplyr::filter(!grepl("-I", gene_id)) %>%
     pull(gene_id)

exon_data <- snrna_data[exon_ids]

intron_ids <- rowData(snrna_data) %>%
     as.data.frame() %>%
     dplyr::filter(grepl("-I", gene_id)) %>%
     pull(gene_id)

intron_data <- snrna_data[intron_ids]

pattern_to_remove <- "\\..*"
replace_string <- ""

exon_ids <- sub(pattern_to_remove, replace_string, exon_ids)
intron_ids <- sub(pattern_to_remove, replace_string, intron_ids)

rownames(exon_data) <- exon_ids
rownames(intron_data) <- intron_ids
rownames(snrna_data) <- sub(pattern_to_remove, replace_string, rownames(snrna_data))

same_ensembl <- intersect(exon_ids, intron_ids)

snrna_data_ids_subset <- rownames(snrna_data) %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%
  dplyr::filter(!. %in% same_ensembl) %>%
  pull(.)

sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays = list(counts = rbind(counts(snrna_data[snrna_data_ids_subset]),
    counts(exon_data[same_ensembl]) + counts(intron_data[same_ensembl]))))

colData(sce) <- colData(snrna_data)
rowData(sce) <- rbind(rowData(snrna_data) %>%
                        as.data.frame() %>%
                        dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% snrna_data_ids_subset),
                      rowData(snrna_data) %>%
                        as.data.frame() %>%
                        dplyr::filter(rownames(.) %in% same_ensembl)
                      )




sce <- sce %>%
    mutate(condition = case_when(str_detect(sample_id, "C") ~ "Control",
                                 str_detect(sample_id, "E") ~ "SleepDeprived"
                                )
          ) %>%
    mutate(replicate = factor(str_remove(sample_id, "C|E")))

map <- AnnotationDbi::mapIds(EnsDb.Mmusculus.v79, keys = rownames(sce), column = "SEQNAME",
                             keytype = "GENEID")
rowData(sce)$CHR <- map
rowData(sce)$is_mito <- case_when(
  rowData(sce)$CHR == "MT"  ~ TRUE,
  .default = FALSE
)

# QC to identify filters

Grabbing the gene names that were used for the heatmaps in Supplemental Figure 5 of the paper.

genes_to_use <- c("Gad1", "Gad2", "Slc17a7", "Sncg", "Vip", "Sst", "Pvalb", "Rorb", "Fezf2", "Foxp2", "Mbp", "Cldn5", "C1qa", "Lhx2", "Sox9", "Etv1", "Gfap", "Tle4", "Nos1", "Htr3a")
features <- rownames(sce)[which(rowData(sce)$SYMBOL %in% genes_to_use)]

Note that I can’t just pass the genes_to_use vector to the function because it’s expecting rownames values which for us are ensembl IDs. If I just use the features to plot the heatmap (the corresponding ensembl IDs), then I can’t display the gene symbol names. However, I can set the swap_rownames argument to the rowData column I want SYMBOL in which case, I need to pass genes_to_use instead of features to the function.

Columns are nuclei
This heatmap plots a select number of genes within the rows and all of the nuclei that were retained after filtering along the columns. We’re specifically plotting the deconvolution normalized expression values.
Simplified example orienting learners to what the heatmap will look like









Can add thought questions about

what the ?, *, &, and ^ cells would represent
why might color be used instead of labeling the cells with numbers?
what would n be in this dataset?
what would m be in this dataset?


scater::plotHeatmap(sce,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "deconvcounts",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL")










We can cluster just the columns (or the nuclei) (rather than the genes as well)

plotHeatmap(sce,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "deconvcounts",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL",
            cluster_rows = FALSE)










Or use no clustering at all

plotHeatmap(sce,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "deconvcounts",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL",
            cluster_rows = FALSE,
            cluster_cols = FALSE)










No matter which approach we use to plot this heatmap where a select number of genes are plotted in the rows and all nuclei retained after filtering are represented in the columns, we can observe how sparse the data is. We’re specifically plotting the deconvolution normalization counts for each of these genes for each of the nuclei. When we utilize some clustering, the non-zero values are clustered together showing neighborhoods of brighter color rather than being intermittently sprinkled throughout the data.


Columns are based on clustering clusters
For this heatmap, we’ll plot expression for genes (represented in rows again), but this time our columns will reflect the expression of that gene for clusters of nuclei. We’ll have to aggregate the counts across the nuclei within each cluster first though.
What are our options for aggregating counts?

Sum gene-specific counts for all nuclei in a cluster
Average gene-specific counts for all nuclei in a cluster

(We’ll provide the clusters and explain how we got them in a click to expand section … may use the Azimuth clusters but for now, using the clusters from the quick cluster approach though each sample will have non-overlapping clusters)

Aggregate by summing

sce_cluster_sums <- scrapper::aggregateAcrossCells.se(sce,
        sce$quickClusters,
        assay.type = "deconvcounts")

This function sums by default without the chance to switch it to averaging, and the scuttle version which lets you specify averaging is deprecated.

plotHeatmap(sce_cluster_sums,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "sums",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL")










Just clustering the columns

plotHeatmap(sce_cluster_sums,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "sums",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL",
            cluster_cols = FALSE)










No clustering at all

plotHeatmap(sce_cluster_sums,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "sums",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL",
            cluster_rows = FALSE,
            cluster_cols = FALSE)













Columns are nuclei pooled for each sample

Aggregate by averaging
Because the aggregateAcrossCells.se function doesn’t natively support averaging, we would have to do it a different way - a few are discussed in this GitHub issues thread

agg <- aggregateAcrossCells.se(sce,
                               sce$sample_id,
                               assay.type = "deconvcounts")
assay(agg, "averages") <- t(t(assays(agg)$sums)/agg$counts)

Alternatively, we can use the sweep function instead of the double transpose step. sce_sample_avgs <- sweep(assays(agg)$sums, MARGIN = 2, STATS = agg$counts, FUN = "/")
Finally, a better approach is to use a tidySingleCellExperiment function for this. (it can also do sums by switching the aggregation_function parameter)

sce_sample_avgs <- sce %>%
    tidySingleCellExperiment::aggregate_cells(
        .sample = sample_id,                    # The colData column to group by
        assays = "deconvcounts",                # The assay to aggregate
        aggregation_function = Matrix::rowMeans # Computes average instead of sum
    )
names(assays(sce_sample_avgs)) <- "averages"

This heatmap shows the average normalized expression pooling all nuclei in a sample together – this visualization is the most similar to the data from bulk RNA-sequencing because it’s ignoring the “single cell/nuclei” aspects of the data.

plotHeatmap(sce_sample_avgs,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "averages",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL",
            colour_columns_by = "condition")










This heatmap only clusters the columns

plotHeatmap(sce_sample_avgs,
            genes_to_use,
            exprs_values = "averages",
            swap_rownames = "SYMBOL",
            cluster_rows = FALSE,
            colour_columns_by = "condition")

text:
Put the process together with pipeComp
We’ll focus on combining the normalization and aggregation processes and ask a few questions about the normalized/aggregated data.

What is the highest expressed gene (within the clusters/samples)? What is its observed normalized expression?

For this we’ll want to look at within cluster/sample normalized expression and find the highest value and report that back. We can figure out which gene is the highest across the most number of clusters/samples. We’ll specifically report back the gene name, how many clusters/samples it’s the highest for, and the observed normalized expression value. We’ll call this "max".

How many genes have no observed normalized expression within a cluster/sample?

For this we’ll want to look within cluster/sample normalized expression values and find how many 0s there are. We can find the quartiles across the clusters/samples and report those numbers back (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100%). We’ll call this "min".

What is the highest observed variance of normalized expression (across the clusters/samples)? Which gene exhibits this amount of variance?

For this we’ll find the variance of each gene’s observed normalized expression across clusters/samples and then return the highest variance observed and which gene has that variance. We’ll call this "variance".

What is the lowest observed median normalized expression (within the clusters/samples)? Which gene is closest to this value?

For this we’ll find the median observed normalized expression value within each cluster/sample. We’ll then find which gene in that cluster/sample that has the closest observed normalized expression. Finally, we’ll pick the lowest value across all the clusters reporting the gene, the median value, and the grouping_id for the cluster or sample that gene was identified for. We’ll call this "median".
We can compare the results of each of these across different combinations of normalization and aggregation.
We’ll want to build some functions with parameters that control the functions/behavior so that we can use pipeComp.
The alternatives/choices we want to work with are

alternatives <- list(
  par1=c("logcounts", "deconvolution"),
  par2=c("sum", "average"),
  par3 = c("cluster", "sample"),
  par4 = c("max", "min", "variance", "median")
)

#' A function to drive the normalization and aggregation process
#'
#' @parameter load_data either TRUE or FALSE. Will load data if TRUE, will run the normalization process if FALSE (unless provided sce has the names associated with the data already)
#' @parameter norm_method either logcounts or deconvolution
#' @parameter sce default is NULL, provide if load_data is FALSE. Should be a SingleCellExperiment object that is filtered but not yet normalized. Should have colData columns `sum` and `sample_id`
#' @parameter aggregation_method either sum or average
#' @parameter aggregation_across either cluster or sample
#' @return sce the SingleCellExperiment object with the newly normalized data saved in either the `logcounts` or `deconvcounts` assay slot


norm_aggregate_data <- function(norm_method, load_data, aggregation_method, aggregation_across, sce = NULL){

  # check parameter inputs
  stopifnot(load_data %in% c(TRUE, FALSE))
  stopifnot(norm_method %in% c('logcounts', 'deconvolution'))
  stopifnot(aggregation_method %in% c('sum', 'average'))
  stopifnot(aggregation_across %in% c('cluster', 'sample'))

  # normalization

  if (load_data){
    sce <- readRDS(here("data/wrangled/sce_norm.rds"))
  } else {
    if (is.null(sce)){
      stop("Must provide an sce object with filtered, unnormalized or normalized data and colData columns `sum` and `sample_id`.")
    }
    if (norm_method == "logcounts"){
      if (!("logcounts" %in% names(assays(sce)))) {
        sce <- scrapper::normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce,
                                           size.factors = sce$sum,
                                           block = sce$sample_id)
      }
    }
    if (norm_method == "deconvolution"){
      if (!("quickClusters" %in% names(colData(sce)) & "deconvcounts" %in% names(assays(sce)))){
        sce$quickClusters <- scran::quickCluster(sce, block = sce$sample_id)
        deconv_sf <- scran::calculateSumFactors(sce, clusters = clusters.block)
        sce <- normalizeRnaCounts.se(sce,
                                 size.factors = deconv_sf,
                                 block = sce$sample_id,
                                 output.name = "deconvcounts",
                                 factor.name = "deconvSizeFactor")
      }
    }
  }

  # aggregation

  if(norm_method == "logcounts"){
    assay_type <- "logcounts"
  } else{
    assay_type <- "deconvcounts"
  }

  if(aggregation_across == "cluster"){
    coi <- "quickClusters"
    if (!coi %in% names(colData(sce))){
      sce$quickClusters <- scran::quickCluster(sce, block = sce$sample_id)
    }
  } else{
    coi <- "sample_id"
  }


  if (aggregation_method == "sum"){
    aggregated <- scrapper::aggregateAcrossCells.se(sce,
                      colData(sce)[[coi]],
                      assay.type = assay_type)
    aoi <- "sums"
  }

  if (aggregation_method == "average"){
    aggregated <- tidySingleCellExperiment::aggregate_cells(sce,
                      .sample = coi,
                      assays = assay_type)
    names(assays(aggregated)) <- "averages"
    aoi <- "averages"
  }

  return (assays(aggregated)[[aoi]])
}

#' A function to grab a specific descriptive stat or metric about the normalized and aggregated data
#'
#' @parameter agg_data the aggregated data
#' @parameter sce Should be a SingleCellExperiment object that is filtered but not yet normalized. Should have colData column `sample_id` or `quickClusters`
#' @parameter aggregation_method either sum or average
#' @parameter aggregation_across either cluster or sample
#' @parameter metric either max, min, variance, or median
#'
#' @return if metric is max the gene ID for the highest expressed gene (seen in the most aggregation_across) (as well as its expression)
#'         if metric is min the average number of genes with no observed expression across the aggregation_across
#'         if metric is variance the gene ID for the highest variance gene for variance across the aggregated clusters or samples (as well as its expression)
#'         if metric is median the gene ID associated with the least median expression observed (as well as the median expression)
#'

grab_metric <- function(agg_data, metric){

  stopifnot(metric %in% c('max', 'min', 'variance', 'median'))

  col_names_res <- c("gene", "gene_count", "gene_avg",
                     "0%", "25%", "50%", "75%", "100%",
                     "median_value", "grouping_id",
                     "variance")

  if (metric == "max"){
    result <- apply(agg_data, 2, function(col) {
      c(gene = rownames(agg_data)[which.max(col)], max_value = max(col))
    }) %>%
      t() %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      group_by(gene) %>%
      summarize(gene_count = n(),
                gene_avg = mean(as.numeric(max_value))) %>%
      slice_max(gene_count, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

  }

  if (metric == "min"){
    result <- colSums(agg_data == 0) %>% quantile() %>% t() %>% as.data.frame()
  }

  if (metric == "variance"){
    result <- apply(agg_data, 1, var) %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      slice_max(as.numeric(`.`), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>%
      dplyr::rename(., variance = `.`) %>%
      mutate(gene = rownames(.))
  }

  if (metric == "median"){
    result <- apply(agg_data, 2, function(col) {
      # Calculate the standard median
      med_val <- round(median(col),2)

      # Find the row index of the value closest to the median
      gene <- rownames(agg_data)[which.min(abs(col - med_val))]

      c(gene = gene, median_value = med_val)
    }) %>%
      t() %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      mutate(grouping_id = as.factor(row_number())) %>%
      slice_min(as.numeric(median_value), n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
  }

  missing_cols <- setdiff(col_names_res, colnames(result))
  result[missing_cols] <- NA

  return(list(result))

}

Putting these functions together into a pipeline that pipeComp can run through with our different parameter alternatives ….

norm_aggregate_pipeline <- pipeComp::PipelineDefinition( list(
  step1 = function(x, par1, par2, par3){
    x <- norm_aggregate_data(par1, FALSE, par2, par3, x)
  },
  step2 = function(x, par4){
    e <- grab_metric(x, par4)
    list(x = x, intermediate_return = e)
    }
  ),
  # 2. Tell pipeComp how to aggregate the metric from step2
  aggregation = list(
    step2 = pipeComp::defaultStepAggregation
  )
)
